articles.title: Republicans’ affordability agenda should start with solar energy
articles.summary: The best way to heed the voters’ mandate is to focus relentlessly on reducing everyday energy costs.
articles.body:
Republicans got beat badly on Election Day. Losing both chambers of Congress while surrendering Senate seats in Republican strongholds like Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi is not a setback that can be explained away by a few disappointing candidates. It is a rejection of how the party has governed.

Voters demanded action on lowering the cost of living, the top issue for the voters who swept President Trump into office and still is at the top of the list for them today . If Republicans are going to regain their confidence, they need a credible plan to reduce costs.

At the center of the party’s midterm repudiation were energy costs, with the war in Iran spiking the price of a gallon of gas by more than $1 . It wasn’t just the price paid at the pump that drove voter anger, but the monthly utility bill. Over the past year , electricity prices rose 4.4 percent, outpacing overall inflation of 3.7 percent. For families already struggling with grocery bills and other expenses, rising electricity costs only added to the squeeze.

The post-midterm reckoning will see a winding down of the war, but voter concerns about affordability ran deeper than just this one issue.

The warning signs were not hidden. In an October survey conducted by my organization, Echelon Insights, 55 percent of likely voters named inflation and the cost of living as a top priority for policymakers. Republicans had every reason to understand what voters wanted Washington to address, starting with the electricity bill.

The best way to heed the voters’ mandate is to focus relentlessly on reducing everyday energy costs. That means expanding domestic energy production and removing barriers to building the infrastructure needed to meet growing demand.

Solar and battery storage belong in that response. Demand for electricity is climbing for the first time in a generation, and the fastest way to keep prices from climbing with it is to add supply quickly. Solar and battery storage can be built faster than any other source, and once running they produce power with no fuel cost.

Where solar and storage have been built at scale, they have pushed down the cost of generating power. In Texas, rapid growth in both helped cut summer wholesale electricity prices by 42 percent between 2021 and 2026, even as demand climbed.

Solar is now the fastest growing source of new power in America, and its cost has fallen dramatically over the last decade. According to the Energy Information Administration, solar and battery storage accounted for roughly four-fifths of new utility-scale capacity added in 2025. An energy strategy that sidelines them would be excluding a substantial part of the country’s new capacity.

There is also little reason to assume voters want Republicans to wage a political campaign against solar. Republicans may be tempted to make renewable energy another casualty of their battles with the new Democratic majorities, but in Echelon’s January survey , 67 percent of likely voters viewed solar energy companies favorably, compared with 14 percent unfavorably.

Republicans do not have to embrace the Democratic climate agenda to let solar compete. But they should distinguish between scoring political points and addressing the affordability concerns voters brought to the ballot box. President Trump helped reshape the Republican Party by bringing working-class voters into the Republican coalition. The election results should be a warning that their support cannot be taken for granted. Keeping them requires delivering on the economic concerns that brought them into the coalition in the first place.

And the consequences of failing to do so will linger: Republicans will have other chances in 2028, but eight of the nine Senate seats they lost won’t be back on the ballot until 2032 .

Making another chance at a unified government a prerequisite for progress would compound the mistake. Republicans cannot afford to spend the next two years waiting for Democrats to fail. Families should not have to wait for Washington’s preferred political arrangement to get a serious response.

Congress has an immediate opportunity to act. Bipartisan permitting legislation is on the table right now, and the Senate already got the job done, passing it 62 to 33 . Finishing that work in the lame duck would demonstrate that the election produced something more than a new round of partisan warfare, while making it easier to build the domestic energy infrastructure America needs.

The election was a reminder that voters have little patience for political games when their own bills keep climbing. Republicans and Democrats may disagree about how to lower those costs, but neither can afford to confuse blocking the other party with solving the problem. On the rising cost of living, that means making room for affordable American power, including solar and storage, rather than letting political disagreements stand in the way.

The election may be over, but the affordability crisis isn’t. Washington needs to stop keeping score of political victories when American families are keeping score of their bills.

Patrick Ruffini is a founding partner at Echelon Insights.

articles.title: Holder says 2028 Democratic presidential candidates must campaign for restoring US as a 'DEI-infused nation'
articles.summary: Obama Attorney General Eric Holder says no Democrat can win the 2028 nomination without pledging to return America to a "DEI-infused nation."
articles.body: Obama-era Attorney General Eric Holder suggested that any Democrat who wants to win in 2028 needs to campaign to restore America to being a "DEI-infused nation" once again. Holder appeared on Monday’s episode of MS Now host Nicolle Wallace’s "The Best People" podcast, where they talked about how the Democratic Party should respond to the impact of the second Trump administration and chart a new course for America going forward. "What do you see in the crop of 2028 Democratic presidential candidates that gives you hope that we're not just going to get through these two years but potentially head to something better?" Wallace asked. "Because I don't think a person can be nominated as the next Democratic candidate for president who won't say, ‘What has happened before is unacceptable. This is my plan to get us back to, you know, a DEI-infused nation. We're going to confront our history. We're going to make our political system more fair. We're going to hold accountable to the extent that we can people who did inappropriate things in the prior four years,’" he said. DEMOCRATS SIZE UP 2028 IN DENVER. WE ASKED WHO’S READY TO RUN He added, "I don't think a Democratic candidate can win the nomination without saying those things and then actually hope for re-election without doing those kinds of things and I think the American people are looking for fighters." Wallace went on to agree that voters have been seeking such leaders for years, caring less about how far left they are. "This is the piece that I feel like the media still gets wrong as well. People have said, ‘Aren't you worried about how left some Democrats are?’ And my audience, that I'm not sure that I understand all their politics, what they are drawn to like almost 100% of the time is the people fighting," she said. Earlier in the interview, Holder criticized the rhetoric of "’Make America Great Again’" and asked, "When did you think America was great? I mean, really? Is it like the ‘Leave it to Beaver’ years when June Cleaver was vacuuming with pearls?" He added, "That was a time when, you know, Black folks were segregated, women were relegated then to household work, people in the LGBT community were in the closet. That's when you think America was great. No, America's great in its present form, or greater." KAMALA HARRIS URGES DEMS TO 'BE RUTHLESS' WITH POWER AFTER MIDTERMS, DEMANDS TRUMP ACCOUNTABILITY He then checked himself, noting that America may not be so great under Trump’s leadership, but said even now, it is ultimately better than it was in past eras. He added that those who appeal to America’s past "look back to an America that is kind of mythical, but never really existed, that's what they're really trying to do here. And I think we have to, every now and again, pull back and try to see the big picture of what these folks are trying to do. And that is chief among the reasons why we have to oppose them, and we use the political system to do it." White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster talked to Fox News Digital: "President Trump was resoundingly elected with a mandate to end divisive, racist policies and restore merit and efficiency. DEI ran rampant during the Biden Administration, and Americans ultimately paid the price for these destructive policies with a restricted labor pool, higher operational costs, and workforce inefficiencies. The Trump Administration will always promote equal treatment under the law for every American, regardless of race or ethnicity." Theo Wold, a former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy during Trump's first term, spoke to Fox News Digital about the exchange, arguing this is the Democratic Party revealing its true agenda after winning the midterms on affordability. "This is right on cue. Democrats ran on affordability and anti-corruption, but that was a ruse to convince voters," he said. "Once they are in office, the goal is to 'infuse' the country with DEI because their real goal is a radical revolution that overturns and replaces our historic institutions and enshrines a race-based policy that caters to their favorite interest groups and voting blocs. articles.title: Trump heads to Arizona next week to speak at a semiconductor manufacturing plant
articles.summary: President Donald Trump will travel to Arizona on Dec. 4 to speak at the groundbreaking for a new Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. plant.
articles.body: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump, who has staked his economic policy on growth in the artificial intelligence sector, will travel to Arizona on Dec. 4 to speak at the groundbreaking for a new Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. computer chip foundry, according to both the White House and the Taiwan-based company. The trip will come at the end of a week where AI comes under the microscope in Washington in the aftermath of Trump intervening to get his ally Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia. Huang is slated to testify at a Senate Banking Committee hearing on Dec. 3 and will face questions about how his company has been selling its chips abroad — and his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Beijing has denied it. TSMC has expanded aggressively in the Phoenix, Arizona, area, using its U.S. facilities to manufacture chips for tech companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Broadcom, and Qualcomm. Trump is attending the start of construction on the fifth phase of TSMC’s expansion in Arizona. TSMC in July announced plans to spend another $100 billion on expanding its manufacturing capacity in the United States, bringing its total pledged investment in American chipmaking to $265 billion. The size of the investment has grown as the development of artificial intelligence has stimulated demand for more computer chips, at the same time as Taiwan’s dominance in chipmaking has led countries including the U.S. to address supply chain vulnerabilities by producing more domestically. While Trump has sought to promote the investments as a function of his tariffs, the company began construction in Arizona during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden. The bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act, signed into law by Biden, also helped to provide some financial support for the project. The White House said the expansion would enable the creation of 10,000 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs in the wider community. The site currently accounts for more than 12,000 construction jobs.

articles.title: The revolution created under Lyndon Johnson was resurrected in 2026
articles.summary: His third great revolution stands on the precipice of a final victory.
articles.body:
In 1965, Lyndon B. Johnson signed two historic measures: The Hart-Cellar Act and the Voting Rights Act . Those measures became the third great revolution in American history following the Revolutionary and the Civil Wars.

The Hart-Cellar Act removed the severe limitations enacted by a Republican-controlled Congress in 1924 that set 2 percent limits to the number of migrants that could enter the United States from the countries listed in the 1890 census. Prior to his assassination, John F. Kennedy called those quotas “without basis in either logic or reason.” Assuming the presidency upon Kennedy’s assassination, Johnson vowed to translate Kennedy’s proposed bill into law.

And he made good on that promise. After Johnson signed the legislation under the gaze of Lady Liberty, a wave of immigrants, larger than any other in history, entered the U.S. Today , there are 53.3 million foreign-born residents living in the U.S., with 11 million having arrived between 2020 and 2025.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Passage of the Hart-Cellar Act was just one part of Johnson’s revolution. A few months earlier, he muscled through Congress the Voting Rights Act. The statute stipulated that Southern states must seek pre-clearance from the Justice Department before redrawing their congressional districts. It further enabled federal examiners to intervene and add African Americans to the voting rolls.

Five years after its passage, almost as many African Americans registered to vote in six Southern states as in the entire century before 1965. Black representation in Congress increased exponentially and several Southern states redrew congressional lines to create majority-minority districts.

After signing the law, Johnson confided to his press secretary, Bill Moyers, “We may have lost the South for your lifetime—and mine.” He was right. Johnson died in 1973; Moyers died in 2025.

Donald Trump came to office determined to undo Johnson’s revolution. Like the Republicans of 1924, Trump preferred immigrants from “nice countries like Denmark or Switzerland.” Decrying the vast number of non-white migrants that came to the U.S. after 1965, Trump denounced them as “poisoning the blood of the country.”

Trump also took aim at the Voting Rights Act, a law that Johnson said corrected a wrong “which no American, in his heart, can justify.”

Thanks to three Trump-appointed Supreme Court justices, the Louisiana v. Callais decision declared that majority Black congressional districts drawn after passage of the Voting Rights Act constituted an unlawful racial gerrymander. Southern states immediately began redrawing their district lines to eliminate Black congressional representation. Louisiana was the first, erasing a majority Black district . Other states vowed to follow Louisiana’s example.

But in 2026, voters resuscitated Johnson’s revolution. In majority-minority counties subject to protections guaranteed by the 1965 Voting Rights Act, turnout was 10 percent higher than in 2022.

Mississippi elected the first Black senator since Reconstruction. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first African American woman to be elected governor of Georgia. Democrats David Crowley and Aaron Ford became the first African American governors in Wisconsin and Nevada, and Wes Moore was easily reelected in Maryland. And Byron Donalds, a Republican, became the first Black governor of Florida.

Hispanic turnout also reached record levels. In California, Hispanic voters jumped from 28 percent in 2022 to 41 percent in 2026. Xavier Becerra became the state’s first Hispanic governor in over 150 years .

In Texas, majority Hispanic communities along the Mexican border reversed the gains Republicans made in 2024 and ousted several GOP members of Congress. A Hispanic woman, Gina Hinjosa, became the first Democrat to win the Texas governorship since 1990, and the first Latina governor of the state. Nationwide, there was a 33-point shift of Hispanic non-college voters to the Democrats.

In a January interview with The New York Times, Trump denounced Johnson’s civil rights legislation as creating an era where “white people were very badly treated.” When Trump promised to “ Make America Great Again ,” what he really meant was recreating the good old days where whites were an overwhelming majority, Blacks were subjugated in the South and Hispanics constituted a very small proportion of the population. Those who felt most threatened by Johnson’s revolution rallied to Trump’s banner.

When Johnson signed the 1965 Voting Rights Act, he told the assembled members of Congress: “It is difficult to fight for freedom. But I also know how difficult it can be to bend long years of habit and custom to grant it.”

Despite numerous setbacks, and Trump’s determined effort to restore the long years of habit and custom, the fight for freedom has finally given way to fulfilling Johnson’s dream of a multi-cultural, multi-racial America where his third great revolution stands on the precipice of a final victory.

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at The Catholic University of America who writes on Substack . His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “ Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics.”

articles.title: 2026's biggest political turkeys: Scandals, gaffes and other memorable unfortunate moments from this year
articles.summary: Eric Swalwell's California gubernatorial collapse, Tim Walz's fraud scandal and more: the political figures whose 2026 ended in scandal and defeat.
articles.body: As 2026 comes to a close, several political blunders, missteps, and serious allegations have left prominent politicians and notable figures presumably looking back with regret. Here are the top political turkeys who made headlines for unfortunate reasons this year. Eric Swalwell Heading into 2026, Eric Swalwell was a well-known member of Congress and the leading Democratic contender in the race for governor of California. By March, he had become the frontrunner in the race and looked poised to take control of the nation’s largest economy in a state where Democrats rarely lose in statewide general elections. Shortly after, that all changed when allegations of sexual assault and other misconduct surfaced in April, prompting prominent Democrats to swiftly withdraw their endorsements and call for Swalwell to abandon his gubernatorial bid. SWALWELL’S FORMER DEM RIVAL UNLOADS ON HIS ‘LIGHTWEIGHT’ CAREER AS SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS EMERGE Swalwell denied the sexual assault allegations, but within days he suspended his campaign and resigned from Congress amid bipartisan calls for his ouster, which effectively ended his political career and put him in potential legal jeopardy. Swalwell faces a federal investigation and separate probes in New York and Los Angeles into sexual assault allegations, which he denies. FBI agents seized his electronic devices and searched his Washington home in August, and in October searched a Beverly Hills mansion where he had stayed. No criminal charges have been filed. Tim Walz In 2024, Walz was elevated to the top of the national scene when he was chosen by former Vice President Kamala Harris to be her running mate for president. Since then, Walz’s political fortunes have taken a downward turn after the Harris-Walz ticket lost the presidential election, leading some pundits to criticize the decision to add him to the ticket. In January 2026, Walz’s political career took another hit when he announced he was dropping his bid for re-election as governor amid a massive fraud scandal that is estimated to have cost the state billions. Polling in June showed that Walz’s approval rating had dropped to its lowest level since he took office. ANGER SWELLS AFTER SWALWELL'S 'OPEN SECRET' WITH WOMEN WENT UNREPORTED FOR YEARS Republicans in Congress Republicans faced historical headwinds heading into the midterm elections and were dealing with significant voter frustration on issues like gas prices and affordability. While many expected Democrats to have a good night on Nov. 3, the GOP ended up losing control of both chambers of Congress ahead of President Donald Trump’s final two years in office. Additionally, Democrats picked up control of the majority of governorships in the United States as well as control of the majority of state legislatures, giving the party a dominant presence it hasn’t seen in decades. Axios reported that 75% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic governor and 53% live in a state where Democrats control the legislature and the governorship. TIM WALZ SAYS HE TAKES RESPONSIBILITY FOR MINNESOTA FRAUD BY NOT RUNNING FOR RE-ELECTION Jasmine Crockett After years as one of the most recognizable and outspoken Democratic members of Congress, Crockett will be out of a job on Capitol Hill in 2027 after opting against House re-election to pursue an unsuccessful Senate bid. Her decision followed Texas Republicans’ redrawing of the congressional map, which reduced the number of Democratic-leaning seats in the Dallas-Fort Worth area from three to two and scrambled the plans of three Democratic incumbents. Crockett’s redrawn 30th District remained Democratic-leaning, but she chose a statewide campaign rather than seeking another House term. Crockett lost the Democratic primary to state Rep. James Talarico in March, then reignited tensions by describing the contest as a "racist race" and pushed back against expectations that she would campaign alongside him. "People keep trying to say, ‘Well, Jasmine has to go and hold his hand.’ No, I don’t," she said during a July podcast appearance, arguing that supporting Black candidates further down the ballot would help increase turnout. Although Crockett and her campaign said she had endorsed Talarico through her post-primary call to support the Democratic ticket, her reluctance to campaign with him and his omission from her political action committee’s endorsements fueled questions about her enthusiasm. Talarico defended her, saying he welcomed her endorsement, while Crockett maintained that elevating lesser-known candidates would benefit Democrats on the ballot. Talarico ultimately defeated Republican Ken Paxton by about 12 percentage points, becoming the first Texas Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat there since Lloyd Bentsen was re-elected in 1988. Francesca Hong The socialist Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate was dominating in the polls heading into the August Democratic primary, but her campaign stumbled in its final days as she struggled to explain past calls to cancel Thanksgiving before narrowly losing to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a candidate who had exited and then returned to the race. The controversy centered on a resurfaced 2020 social media post in which Hong wrote, "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," and criticized celebrating colonialism. Asked on CNN in August whether she still wanted the holiday canceled, Hong initially emphasized that Thanksgiving was painful for some communities rather than directly rejecting her earlier position. She later reversed course, saying she loved Thanksgiving and did not want to cancel it. After losing the primary, Hong acknowledged that she regretted the CNN interview. Cindy Hyde-Smith The Republican senator lost her seat in deep-red Mississippi to Democrat Scott Colom after an answer about rising beef prices became damaging campaign fodder. Asked by WLOX anchor Hugh Keeton about rising beef prices during a local television interview, Hyde-Smith responded, "You know, you have so many proteins to choose from." Colom later used the exchange in a campaign ad featuring voters saying they would rather pick another senator. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Colom ultimately defeated Hyde-Smith by just 8,031 votes, a margin of less than 1 percentage point — close enough that her remark, amplified by her opponent’s advertising, could have made the difference in a race that cost Republicans a seat many believed was safe. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich singled out the remark while discussing Republican losses with Larry Kudlow on Fox News before the race was called, arguing that suggesting cheaper food failed to address voters’ economic frustrations. "I mean, it’s not the job of a senator to explain her failure by suggesting a new diet," Gingrich said. Other honorable mentions include Democratic Fayette County Council candidate Jaime West, who was ridiculed by critics who said she appeared to be drunk and slurred her way through attacks on Republicans during a televised candidate forum; Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, whose controversial ad featuring his opponent’s mother drew fierce blowback before he lost his race; and Maine Democratic Senate candidate Graham Platner's fall from grace as he suspended his campaign after being accused of sexual assault.

articles.title: Trump calls the pre-election GDP figures 'fake' and demands an investigation of Commerce Department
articles.summary: (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday accused his Commerce Department of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections...
articles.body:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday accused his Commerce Department of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections, and said he wants to launch an investigation.

Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fails to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.

His latest complaint concerns data issued by the Commerce Department on Wednesday that revised gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3% on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4%.

The department's Bureau of Economic Analysis routinely updates its economic data to improve their accuracy. GDP figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a pre-scheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.

But the president claimed on social media that it was a "massive, and purposeful, error" and linked it to the poor performance for Republicans in the Nov. 3 midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress.

"It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the Government Agency that does these numbers," Trump posted. "Why wasn't the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation."

The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The government is largely closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.

It's the latest instance of Trump questioning the integrity of economic data he feels is unfavorable to him without providing evidence that revisions are politically motivated. In August 2025, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a decidedly weak jobs report. That report said only 73,000 jobs were added in July 2025 and showed that 258,000 fewer jobs were added in May and June than previously reported.

Trump called that jobs report "phony" and "rigged."

Trump has claimed that he deserves credit for powering stronger economic growth, but voters do not share the president's belief that the economy is strong. In the midterms, 76% described economic conditions as "not so good" or "poor," according to the AP Voter Poll, an extensive survey of the electorate. About two-thirds of voters said Trump's own policies had fueled inflation.

The president in his social media post ignored that the same federal agency on Wednesday also reported that a key measure of inflation — the personal consumption expenditures price index — accelerated to an annual pace of 3.8% in October.

articles.title: America is back at war, and Americans are still at the mall
articles.summary: Retired Marine Corps Lieutenant Colonel Kevin M. Schmiegel argues that local communities must move beyond symbolic gestures like Veterans Day parades to create actionable plans that help service members and their families thrive through employment, mentorship, and integration.
articles.body:
Earlier this month, on Veterans Day, the nation paused to thank those who have served. In America’s 250th year, the gratitude was genuine: parades, free meals, a handshake in an airport terminal. And then, as it does every November, the moment passed.

Five years ago, as we marked the 20th anniversary of 9/11, I wrote in these pages that a rising number of those who shouldered the burden of two decades of war felt increasingly disconnected from their communities and civilian neighbors. I borrowed a line Tom Nichols captured in The Atlantic , a refrain common among the troops in those early years: “We’re at war. America’s at the mall.”

With American service members once again deployed in combat operations this year, I wish I could report that the line has aged poorly. It hasn’t.

The evidence of the military-civilian divide remains compelling and deeply troubling. The 2025 Reagan National Defense Survey found that just 49 percent of Americans have a great deal of confidence in the military, down 21 points since 2018. Fewer Americans have any personal tie to service at all. Pew Research found that only one-third of adults under 30 had an immediate family member who had served. The Department of Defense and its senior leaders have repeatedly characterized this widening gap as a threat to national security, and the reason is simple: young people rarely aspire to a life they have never seen up close.

The hard truth is that data and awareness without subsequent action are meaningless. For too long we’ve patted ourselves on the back for identifying and giving name to an issue. We’re comfortable getting loud about it for a little while, but when it comes time to take that problem off its pedestal and really put our hands on it, the crowd goes quiet. We are failing, time and again, to put our discussion to work to drive action.

I have spent much of the past three years in working sessions between veterans and their families and employers, college presidents, mayors, installation commanders and service providers.

First, the divide is local, and so is the fix. What a transitioning Marine needs in San Diego is not what a Guard family needs in Nashville. National awareness campaigns matter, but the communities making real progress are the ones that stopped waiting for Washington and wrote their own plans: who hires, who trains, who mentors, and how they will measure whether any of it worked.

Second, we have to retire the broken-veteran narrative. When communities see service members, veterans, and military spouses primarily as people to be helped, they design programs. When they see them as students, employees, entrepreneurs, and civic leaders, they design economies. Our goal should be veterans and families who are thriving because of their service, not in spite of it.

Third, thriving is about more than a job. In forum after forum, people described the same pieces: meaningful work, a sense of purpose, a connected community, health and wellness, and the practical tools to navigate a new place. Get one of those right and the others still fail, and the family moves on. Get them right together and families put down roots.

Getting this right is how we inspire the next generation to serve. The most persuasive recruiter in America is not an advertisement, it is a neighbor. When a 16-year-old knows the veteran who owns the HVAC company down the street, the military spouse who teaches her chemistry class, or the Marine who sits on the city council, service becomes a path she can picture for herself.

So here is my ask, in this 250th year. Every member of Congress, mayor, CEO, college president, and installation commander should be able to answer a simple question: what is our community’s plan to make sure those who serve, and their families, thrive here? If the honest answer is a Veterans Day parade, it is time to convene the people who can write a better one, and to invite veterans and military spouses to lead the effort rather than simply be its beneficiaries. If done repeatedly in communities nationwide, these engagements will bridge the civilian-military divide. America doesn’t have to be at the mall. It can be on Main Street.

Kevin M. Schmiegel is a retired Marine Corps lieutenant colonel and co-founder and CEO of ZeroMils.

articles.title: 5 questions facing President Trump this Thanksgiving
articles.summary: President Trump is facing a transformed political landscape as he begins his final two years in the White House. The Republican Party took a serious beating in the midterm elections, with Democrats gaining nine seats in the Senate and notching their highest number of House seats since the 1990s. At least some blame for the…
articles.body:
President Trump is facing a transformed political landscape as he begins his final two years in the White House.

The Republican Party took a serious beating in the midterm elections, with Democrats gaining nine seats in the Senate and notching their highest number of House seats since the 1990s.

At least some blame for the defeat accrued to Trump, who stands near his lowest ebb in opinion polls. Once the new Congress is sworn in, Democrats are sure to launch investigations into his allies and family members. They will also have the power to block the president legislatively.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

But Trump has cards to play, too. He retains the avid support of his MAGA base, he is in firm control of the GOP — most of the time — and his capacity to drive the media agenda is undimmed.

Here are five pressing questions facing Trump this Thanksgiving.

The Iran war, which Trump launched in conjunction with Israel at the end of February, turned out to be an anvil around the GOP’s hopes in the midterms. The spike in energy prices it caused left many voters dismayed, while some erstwhile Trump supporters also regarded it as a betrayal of his “America First” campaign pledges.

Vice President Vance notably blamed the midterms meltdown squarely on the conflict.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote in a social media post on the morning after Election Day.

Trump has insisted he does not object to his vice president’s characterization — though he has suggested that Vance should have affirmed that going to war was the right decision.

Now, the question is where things go from here.

Trump has shifted Vance away from potential new negotiations with the leadership of Iran, writing on social media , “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”

Numerous reports have suggested that an escalation of military action is being seriously contemplated.

It’s also plausible that Trump never gives the green light to that option, instead hoping that Iran’s economic situation becomes more and more desperate. The best-case scenario for the president in that regard is that hardship either leads the Iranian leadership to offer new concessions or sparks some kind of popular uprising.

But two things remain unclear: what, specifically, Trump is seeking to end the war, and whether he might at some point simply declare victory and move on.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) has become the unlikely advocate of some kind of grand bargain between Trump and the Democrats on healthcare.

Trump assailed El-Sayed, who will soon become the nation’s first Muslim senator, in Islamophobic terms during the midterm campaign. Trump several times referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist.”

But El-Sayed, a fervent advocate for “Medicare for All,” has signaled that he would have no problem if Trump plastered his name over such a deal. El-Sayed has insisted , in the face of some skepticism, that his proposal of “Trumpcare” is serious, so long as the underlying policy meets his objectives.

Trump ruffled feathers within his own party when he amplified an El-Sayed post on the topic that included images of a gold card for recipients of the hypothetical program.

Despite all this, the chances of such an expansive agreement seem extremely slim. But Trump did name healthcare, along with college sports reform and boosting the movie and TV production industry, as possible areas of bipartisan agreement in remarks at a Nov. 20 White House news conference.

Even so, it is just as likely that Trump could zigzag away from compromise in favor of renewed attacks on an opposition party he often characterizes as radical and even subversive.

There were signs of that approach two days after the White House press conference, when Trump wrote on social media that he would find it “very hard” to work with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) if Schumer becomes majority leader in January.

Does Jensen Huang’s return stop the AI stock slide?

Plenty has already been said about Trump’s extraordinary intervention to get Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of chip giant Nvidia.

It is widely accepted that Trump’s motivation, at least in part, was to buoy the financial markets. The key question is: Will it work?

Nvidia stocks soared by more than 30 percent on Monday, the first day of trading after it was announced that Huang would return. The company lifted the major stock indices, particularly the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite, up along with it.

But trading screens flashed red once again the following day, as Nvidia dropped almost 6 percent while the Nasdaq declined roughly 1.5 percent.

On one hand, the declines were more modest than the previous day’s gains. On the other, both Nvidia and the broader market are well below their October highs.

The tumult in the markets reflects a confluence of worries. Spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure could slow. Democratic control of Congress, allied with public unease about data centers, could erect regulatory roadblocks. Huang and Nvidia will face further probes, and any bad news could percolate through an AI sector that Nvidia plays a key role in financing.

Alternatively, all of those fears could prove overblown, and bullishness over AI could lift the markets to even loftier heights.

Nobody really knows. Whichever way things break, it will have a significant effect on Trump’s political fortunes.

Is Trump finally slipping toward lame-duck status?

Trump has held off lame-duck status for longer than most second-term presidents.

In part that is testament to his hold on the GOP, and the price that he has exacted on those within the party who have crossed him.

This year, foes like Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), and those who were merely judged insufficiently loyal like Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), were defeated in primaries by Trump-backed challengers.

Still, Trump’s preferred candidate in the Senate race in Texas, state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), went down in a stunning defeat by Sen.-elect James Talarico (D). Trump sustained an electoral black eye by proxy.

The sense that Trump has become an electoral liability to the party emboldened more Republicans than usual to speak out over the Huang controversy. The pattern could be replicated on other issues in the future.

Meanwhile, speculation continues to bubble about the two presumed front-runners to supplant Trump as the GOP’s 2028 nominee — Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

To be sure, Trump won’t be entirely sidelined anytime soon. But after the midterms, a post-Trump era suddenly seems a lot closer.

Trump is in bad shape in the polls. According to The Hill’s polling and data partner Decision Desk HQ, the president’s approval rating was 26 points into negative territory on Monday, with 62 percent of Americans disapproving of his job performance and just 36 percent approving.

It’s quite possible to sketch a scenario in which Trump’s ratings begin to rise again. A definitive end to the Iran war, a drop in inflationary pressure and a brightening economy would all do the trick.

Equally obviously, none of those things is guaranteed.

Meanwhile, Democratic investigations could expose new elements of wrongdoing. And there is a broader suspicion that the sliver of American voters still in the center ground may be tiring of the president’s antics, from his bellicose social media posts to his penchant for self-aggrandizing building projects

All of that being said, Trump has been written off innumerable times before. He may yet have another surprise in store.

articles.title: Nate Silver: Trump could ‘absolutely’ be removed from office after midterm turmoil
articles.summary: Polling analyst Nate Silver suggested there “absolutely” is a chance that President Trump could be removed from office after the GOP and his administration faced clear backlash during the midterms. On an episode of the “Still Counting” podcast between Silver and fellow co-hosts Galen Druke and Clare Malone, the pundit asked the pair what prediction…
articles.body:
Polling analyst Nate Silver suggested there “absolutely” is a chance that President Trump could be removed from office after the GOP and his administration faced clear backlash during the midterms.

On an episode of the “Still Counting” podcast between Silver and fellow co-hosts Galen Druke and Clare Malone, the pundit asked the pair what prediction markets say about a third Trump impeachment and potential removal ahead of the end of his second term.

“Are they saying it’s like 25 percent? I have not looked,” Druke said, before Silver called his co-host “uncannily accurate.”

Silver, who founded FiveThirtyEight, said it is “entirely reasonable” before Malone rebuffed his assertation, suggesting the president would not get convicted by the upper chamber.

“He could absolutely get removed by the Senate,” Silver said, later adding, “If his approval keeps going down at the rate it is, he’s going to be at whatever, 29 percent, by the end of next year, and like if he’s doing s– to, like, profit off selling [Nvidia] chips to China, abso-f—ing-lutely he could be — and he should be.”

He was referring to the Trump administration’s role in getting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reinstated to his post at the chipmaking firm. Huang initially stepped down amid revelations that he had affairs with multiple women, including one who had contact with Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia’s stock drastically rose Monday morning when the markets closed, though the stock price stumbled downward again later in the week.

Democrats have twice unsuccessfully tried to remove Trump from office, once over whether he directed Ukraine to investigate former President Biden and his family and a second time following the 2020 election and Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack.

Trump was acquitted both times, though seven Senate Republicans joined Democrats during his second trial in voting to convict him.

articles.title: Stop chasing billionaires — fix the broken corporate tax system instead
articles.summary: Asking why the billionaire tax failed is the wrong question. Instead, consider why California needed it in the first place.
articles.body:
The defeat of California’s billionaire asset tax proposal earlier this month is a puzzle. And while the key to that puzzle may be less believable than the conspiratorial notion that birds are actually government surveillance drones , this absurdity happens to be true.

As American voters were delivering a stinging rebuke to a party seen as putting the interests of wealthy insiders ahead of ordinary Americans, Californians rejected the modest step of imposing a one-time levy on the holdings of individuals with near-unimaginable wealth . Deep-red Texas elected Democrats by stunning margins , but its reliably blue neighbor chose to shield tech moguls from the threat of health care and education spending.

The go-to explanation has been political spending. Billionaires certainly did spend vast amounts to defeat the tax. But opponents of Sherrod Brown heavily outspent supporters as he trounced his Republican opponent. And gleeful critics note that Elon Musk poured money into the campaign of Republican Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, only to watch him lose by double digits. Money alone could not turn back this particular blue wave.

Asking why the billionaire tax failed is the wrong question. Instead, consider why California needed it in the first place. The conventional answer focuses on obstacles to a national wealth tax, including valuation and constitutional hurdles . The real problem lies elsewhere, which is how we find ourselves in birds-aren’t-real territory.

The challenges of creating a national wealth tax are clear. The Constitution could demand apportionment — don’t ask — since a wealth tax might stray beyond the protection of the 16th Amendment . Navigating apportionment might be no easier than ratifying a whole new constitutional amendment.

An anemic federal estate tax raises the question of whether such heroics would even be worth it. That tax raises less than 1 percent of federal revenue each year. Whether a victim of congressional apathy or ruthless planning by the handful of wealthy Americans it targets, it’s hard to imagine that pursuing those same elites while alive would produce better results.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) recently embraced a different approach. Rather than waiting to tax the winners of today’s AI sweepstakes after they have secured their fortunes, Sanders proposed a tax on the companies themselves . His tax on — or rather in — the equity of mammoth AI ventures could unlock an enormous trove of revenues without straying into constitutional minefields or chasing after elusive billionaires.

Sanders’s revolutionary approach: tax corporations. But don’t we already do that?

We do, of course. But the corporate tax has a problem not so different than California’s failed tax. Had it been enacted, California’s tax would have invited billionaires to relocate . But corporations can’t escape a federal corporate tax by moving across state lines.

We are told that they can hide their profits overseas . In fact, governments around the world have spent decades and millions upon millions of dollars building a complex system designed to prevent the taxation of the world-spanning corporations that created today’s billionaires. A global tax system, more than half a century after its inception, remains deeply entrenched, incredibly potent and, most importantly, almost entirely unnoticed.

Beginning in the 1960s, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development built a vast network of international agreements that has made it difficult for all countries — and, all too predictably, poor countries in particular — to tax multinational corporations. The treaties can reduce or entirely eliminate taxes on profits paid from one country to another, and they forbid taxes on corporations without a “permanent establishment” in a country. Today, more than ever, a business can earn vast profits in a country without offices, warehouses or factories, and pay absolutely no tax there.

We should mourn the California billionaire tax. But we should also take its failure as an invitation to dismantle the hidden mechanism that made it necessary. I would rather tax corporations than their entitled owners anyway.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin personally spent more than $100 million to defeat the billionaire tax. It’s a vast amount for any one person, yet the effort barely left a ripple in his oceanic fortune. Brin’s wealth, although rooted in technology, also owes a debt to abusive tax strategies such as the once-popular double Irish Dutch sandwich.

That technique — Apple used it as well — would not have been possible without those international agreements. As the name suggests, they eliminated taxes on profits routed through Irish and Dutch subsidiaries of giant tech companies.

If you want to collect the taxes needed to fund urgent priorities like health care and education, that should come as relief as well as a surprise. Rather than dreaming up an entirely new tax, we can simply stop spending millions to protect billionaires from the corporate tax we already have.

Steven Dean, author of “Racial Capitalism and International Tax Law: The Story of Global Jim Crow,” is professor of law and Paul Siskind Research Scholar at Boston University School of Law and serves on the board of the Economic Hardship Reporting Project.

articles.title: Thanksgiving has a bumpy history
articles.summary: The history of the American Thanksgiving holiday has evolved from early colonial feasts and Revolutionary War era proclamations to modern debates over its religious nature and official date.
articles.body:
Happy Thanksgiving! That holiday greeting may seem nongermane to a Congress blog, but it is not. Just as the contemporary turkey day is practically synonymous with wall-to-wall pigskin games on television, historically the national celebration became something of a political football. Before you squeal and cry fowl, let me explain.

From grade school, we are all familiar with the origins of America’s Thanksgiving. The Pilgrims in the Massachusetts Bay colony, having landed on our shores in November1620 after an arduous 66-day voyage across the Atlantic on the Mayflower, were grateful for their safe arrival. In 1621, they invited their indigenous Wampanoag neighbors to join them in a harvest feast of celebration. In 1623, they held a similar celebration after a prolonged drought.

Fast forward to our revolutionary war. The Continental Congress crafted the first national proclamation of thanksgiving in 1777 in their temporary quarters in York, Pa. The draft of the proclamation, penned by Sam Adams, thanked the “Almighty God” for the blessings bestowed upon them and implored him “to smile upon us in the prosecution of a just and necessary war…and to crown our arms with the most signal success.”

Not to be outdone, Gen. George Washington, leading our revolutionary forces, proclaimed in December 1777 that thanksgiving should be a victory celebration honoring the defeat of the British in the battle of Saratoga.

During its existence from 1774 to 1789, the Continental Congress issued several proclamations designating “national days of prayer, humility, and thanksgiving.” This practice continued under our new government.

Shortly after the first House of Representatives adopted the First Amendment to the Constitution guaranteeing the freedom of speech, the press, and religion in 1789, Rep. Elias Boudinot of New Jersey proposed that the House and Senate request President Washington to proclaim a day of thanksgiving “for the many signal favors of Almighty God.”

Washinton obliged by issuing the first proclamation of Thanksgiving Day by the national government, to be observed on Thursday, Nov. 26, 1789. His successor as president, John Adams, followed suit.

Thomas Jefferson, on the other hand, our third president, refused to issue any proclamation. As a deist, he explained his reasoning in an 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptist Association . He thought that religiously oriented declarations by government violated our First Amendment’s wall separating church and state and its guarantee of the free practice of religion. “Believing that religion is a matter which lies solely between Man and his God,” he wrote, “the legitimate powers of government reach actions only, and not opinions.”

Jefferson’s successor, James Madison, in 1814, at the end of the War of 1812, resumed the precedent set by Washington and Adams. However, neither of Madison’s two proclamations in 1815 was observed. Instead, states like Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and New York began celebrating their own thanksgiving days on dates of their choosing.

It wasn’t until the middle of the Civil War that President Abraham Lincoln, the first president since Madison’s proclamations, began the regular practice of issuing annual Thanksgiving Proclamations. In 1870, President Ulysses S. Grant signed into law the Holidays Act that designated specific federal holidays in Washington, D.C., including New Year’s, July 4, and Christmas, though Thanksgiving was left to the discretion of the president.

One of the more interesting tugs-of-war over Thanksgiving occurred under President Franklin Roosevelt. With encouragement from Fred Lazarus, Jr., founder of the Federated Department Stores, Roosevelt in 1939 proposed making Thanksgiving the fourth Thursday of November instead of Lincoln’s “final Thursday.” Because it was considered inappropriate to advertise goods for Christmas before Thanksgiving, Roosevelt thought allowing an extra week between the holidays would help lift the economy out of the Great Depression and be a boon to merchants and workers alike.

On Oct. 6, 1941, the U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill that embraced Lincoln’s final Thursday in November as Thanksgiving. However, two months later, the Senate amended the bill switching the date back to the fourth Thursday. The House, after considerable debate, eventually caved and accepted the Senate amendment . And that’s how it still stands today.

This whole tempest in a turkey pot had devolved into a partisan hissing match, with Democrats referring to Nov. 30 as the “Republican Thanksgiving,” and Republicans referring to Nov. 23 as the “Democratic Thanksgiving” or “Franksgiving.”

Who would have thought that this day of family gatherings, peace, and gratefulness was once a source of wartime invocations of the Almighty, First Amendment feuds, and partisan pettiness? Be thankful for today’s gridiron clashes.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran, culminating as chief-of-staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of, “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial,” and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays.”

The document is scheduled to be sold at auction at Christies New York on November 14, 2013. (AP Photo/Matt Rourke)

articles.title: Politics, money and Thanksgiving dinner: Just two words can help avoid argument
articles.summary: Dr. Joel Davis Brown says swapping "yes, but" for "yes, and" can keep Thanksgiving dinner talk civil as post-midterm politics turn tense at the table.
articles.body: As Americans across the country sit down to Thanksgiving dinner just weeks after Democrats' midterm sweep drastically reshaped the political landscape going into 2027, conversations about politics and the economy could turn tense. Dr. Joel Davis Brown, a leadership expert, executive coach and author who studies how people communicate and navigate conflict, says swapping out the word "but" when discussing controversial topics can help keep the discussions civil. "‘But’ shows disagreement," Brown told Fox News Digital. "It’s a way of telling the person that what they said should not be heard, and it really stifles conversation." Instead, Brown suggests trying "yes, and." That doesn’t mean you have to agree, he said. Rather it signals that you’ve heard the other person and leaves room to share a different view. "‘Yes, I’ve heard you and I have a different opinion,’" Brown said. "We can listen to varying opinions." FOOD PRICES ARE RISING BEFORE THANKSGIVING. AN ECONOMIST SHARES WAYS TO SAVE If a hot-button topic comes up, Brown recommends asking the person to "tell me more about that." The question, he says, can help you understand how someone arrived at their view instead of turning the exchange into a debate. He also cautions against opening with "I disagree," which can put people "in an oppositional place" before they have fully heard one another. Rather than trading facts and figures to win an argument, he said, people may make more headway by sharing personal stories and listening to the experiences behind someone else’s opinion. "If you’re going into these exchanges as looking to win an argument, maybe change your approach," Brown said. "Maybe instead of trying to win that argument, you try to understand the other person’s perspective." BLACK FRIDAY DEALS ARE EVERYWHERE. HERE’S HOW TO SPOT REAL SAVINGS Brown said it helps to decide in advance what you want from the interaction, whether that’s getting through the meal, building a relationship or persuading someone. That goal can shape how you respond. Political topics aren't the only ones that can get tense when families come together. For personal questions about marriage, children or other life choices, Brown recommends setting expectations before the gathering. Talk with family or friends about what would help everyone feel comfortable, and be clear about what you do and do not want to discuss. Additionally, if a conversation becomes stressful, take a breath, sip water or step away from the table. Brown said people should know their own triggers and remember they are not responsible for managing every interaction. He encourages approaching disagreements with empathy, which he described as listening to another person’s story without taking on their position. "Look at these as learning opportunities," Brown said.

articles.title: Trump unloads on critics in wide-ranging Thanksgiving Day rant
articles.summary: President Trump marked Thanksgiving Day with a lengthy rant on social media in which he lashed out at his political opponents, accused federal officials of releasing “fake” economic numbers and called for the mass expulsion of Somalis from the U.S. In a grievance-filled post on Truth Social, the president began by wishing Americans a happy…
articles.body:
President Trump marked Thanksgiving Day with a lengthy rant on social media in which he lashed out at his political opponents, accused federal officials of releasing “fake” economic numbers and called for the mass expulsion of Somalis from the U.S.

In a grievance-filled post on Truth Social , the president began by wishing Americans a happy Thanksgiving holiday before turning his attention to his call for an investigation into economic data released ahead of the midterm elections.

“I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late showing that the GDP [gross domestic product] was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated,” Trump wrote Thursday.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said Wednesday that the economy grew at an annualized rate of 4.3 percent between July and September, up from its initial estimate of 3.4 percent.

Trump alleged without evidence that the initial GDP estimates were deliberately understated and called for an investigation into the figures earlier Thursday after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in a midterm election cycle dominated by voters’ concerns over inflation and the rising cost of living.

GDP estimates are routinely revised as more comprehensive data becomes available. The BEA is scheduled to release another estimate next month.

Trump also accused Democrats and the “Radical Far Left” of seeking to impose Sharia law in the U.S. court system and force Americans to redistribute their money “so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work.”

The president then turned his attention the Somali community, claiming without evidence that a fraction of the U.S.’s Somali population works without receiving federal aid.

“I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance,” he wrote. “These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately.”

Trump has repeatedly disparaged Minnesota’s Somali community amid federal investigations into widespread fraud involving government-funded social services programs in the state.

The president also touted his renovations to the White House, ripping the media and others who have criticized his changes to the complex, including the construction of a massive ballroom in the East Wing.

“I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House,” he wrote. “Today, it has never looked better, and will soon have the Ballroom that Presidents have sought for over 150 years.”

articles.summary: Los cuatro candidatos ya se encuentran ultimando los detalles con sus equipos
articles.body: El debate electoral a cuatro de las elecciones generales de 2026 se celebra este jueves, 26 de noviembre, y supone el último encuentro televisado entre los principales candidatos antes de los comicios del próximo domingo 29 de noviembre. Organizado por la Academia de Televisión y moderado por María Casado en Madrid Content City (Tres Cantos), reúne a Pedro Sánchez (PSOE), Alberto Núñez Feijóo (PP), Santiago Abascal (Vox) y Ada Colau (Frente Amplio). Uno de los aspectos que siempre causa expectación entre la ciudadanía es la vestimenta de los candidatos, por lo que vamos a analizarla. A diferencia del cara a cara de la semana pasada, donde lució un traje marrón para causar contrate con el plató de tonos neutros, Pedro Sánchez ha elegido uno de color azul con una corbata de color rojo, prácticamente el mismo con el que apareció en el debate de 2023. El objeto que ha acaparado toda la atención ha sido el pin de la Agenda 2030, con el que, según la periodista Carlota Núñez, pretende reflejar su estrategia y presentar su proyecto, el de avance, frente al de recortes que tiene enfrente, compartido por PP y Vox. Además, su elección ha generado muchas reacciones al ser una combinación muy utilizada por Donald Trump, presidente de Estados Unidos. Ada Colau no ha cambiado su estilo habitual y ha llegado a las instalaciones completamente de negro. No obstante, sí ha aparecido con un detalle diferente: una insignia con el logo LGTBIQ+, el cual define a la perfección su programa. En el caso de Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ha optado por un traje clásico con su corbata azul marino de la suerte. Se trata de un detalle importante, ya que en el último debate con Sánchez lució una de color verde oscuro. Finalmente, Santiago Abascal ha optado por un traje con una corbata azul marino, algo que ya muestra diferencias con su puesta en escena en 2023, donde llevaba una americana y camisa. Susana Camacho, experta en comunicación, ha contado que hará uso de un amuleto: una pulsera de San Benito que le regaló un militante.

articles.summary: El líder de la formación verde fue uno de los primeros en llegar a la cita
articles.body: Este jueves, 26 de noviembre, se llevará a cabo el debate a cuatro con motivo de las elecciones del próximo domingo, 29 de noviembre. Pedro Sánchez, del PSOE, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, del PP, Santiago Abascal, de Vox, y Ada Colau, del Frente Amplio, se verán las caras en una cita organizada por la Academia de Televisión, presidida por María Casado, quien será la encargada de moderarlo. El primero en llegar a la cita fue el líder de la formación verde, sobre las 20:20 horas. Lo hizo en su furgoneta con la que recorrió buena parte del país durante la campaña electoral. Abascal portó un traje con una corbata azul marino. Un cambio notorio con respecto a 2023, ya que llevó americana y camisa. Esta corbata, según desveló Susana Camacho, experta en comunicación, en Cuatro en los momentos previos al evento, tiene un significado detrás que refuerza su figura: “La porta para reforzar su perfil presidencial”. Con este complemento, tal y como explicó, Abascal busca proyectar una imagen de candidato preparado para asumir responsabilidades de Gobierno. Por otro lado, la profesional se ha detenido a analizar otros de los elementos que acompañan al líder de VOX y, más allá de la mencionada corbata, hubo uno que le llamó la atención. Camacho desveló que Abascal hará uso de una pulsera de San Benito que le regaló un militante en el año 2018 en Córdoba. Un elemento de carácter religioso que salió a relucir al analizar los objetos personales del dirigente político. Camacho dejó una reflexión: “Es más de rezar que de este tipo de amuletos”. Así pues, el máximo dirigente de la formación verde combinó una puesta en escena más institucional que la de 2023 junto a un elemento de carácter religioso que lleva consigo gracias al regalo que le dio uno de sus militantes.

La Agenda 2030 es un plan de acción global aprobado por 193 países de la Organización de las Naciones Unidas (ONU) en septiembre de 2015 para erradicar la pobreza, proteger el planeta y garantizar la prosperidad antes del año 2030. Este acuerdo internacional se articula a través de los 17 Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible (ODS) –representados por cada uno de los 17 colores de la rueda del pin– y se desglosa en 169 metas concretas que abarcan el desarrollo social, económico y medioambiental. Los 17 Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible (ODS) son: 1. Fin de la pobreza. Erradicar la pobreza extrema y reducir la vulnerabilidad económica. 2. Hambre cero. Poner fin al hambre, lograr la seguridad alimentaria y promover la agricultura sostenible. 3. Salud y bienestar. Garantizar una vida sana y promover el bienestar universal en todas las edades. 4. Educación de calidad. Asegurar una educación inclusiva, equitativa y de calidad para todos. 5. Igualdad de género. Lograr la igualdad entre los géneros y empoderar a todas las mujeres y niñas. 6. Agua limpia y saneamiento. Garantizar la disponibilidad y la gestión sostenible del agua y el saneamiento. 7. Energía asequible y no contaminante. Asegurar el acceso a energías fiables, sostenibles y modernas. 8. Trabajo decente y crecimiento económico. Fomentar el crecimiento económico sostenido, el empleo pleno y el trabajo digno. 9. Industria, innovación e infraestructura. Construir infraestructuras resilientes, promover la industrialización sostenible y fomentar la innovación. 10. Reducción de las desigualdades. Reducir la brecha de desigualdad en y entre los países. 11. Ciudades y comunidades sostenibles. Lograr que las ciudades y los asentamientos humanos sean inclusivos, seguros, resilientes y sostenibles. 12. Producción y consumo responsables. Garantizar modalidades de consumo y producción sostenibles. 13. Acción por el clima. Adoptar medidas urgentes para combatir el cambio climático y sus efectos. 14. Vida submarina. Conservar y utilizar de forma sostenible los océanos, los mares y los recursos marinos. 15. Vida de ecosistemas terrestres. Proteger y restaurar los ecosistemas terrestres, gestionar los bosques de forma sostenible y frenar la pérdida de biodiversidad. 16. Paz, justicia e instituciones sólidas. Promover sociedades pacíficas, facilitar el acceso a la justicia y construir instituciones eficaces. 17. Alianzas para lograr los objetivos. Revitalizar la alianza mundial para el desarrollo sostenible entre gobiernos, sector privado y sociedad civil.

articles.title: Emmer: GOP should have said it wasn’t ‘realistic’ to fix economy in 2 years
articles.summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) said Republicans should have spent the past two years tempering voters’ expectations about how quickly President Trump could turn the economy around, acknowledging that the party ceded the issue of affordability to Democrats ahead of its bruising midterm losses. “We need to take responsibility for our messaging. We did…
articles.body:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) said Republicans should have spent the past two years tempering voters’ expectations about how quickly President Trump could turn the economy around, acknowledging that the party ceded the issue of affordability to Democrats ahead of its bruising midterm losses.

“We need to take responsibility for our messaging. We did not listen to the American people,” Emmer said Tuesday in an interview with Fox 9 Minneapolis-St. Paul.

“When we became the majority with the Senate and the White House, the idea that you were going to fix an economy that had been destroyed under [former President] Joe Biden in two years was not realistic,” he continued. “We should have been sticking with that economic message from day one, and we didn’t do it.”

The Minnesota Republican added that Democrats “did talk to those issues when they talked about affordability,” which resonated with voters who in turn voted Democrats back into power in the House and Senate.

His remarks come as Republicans reckon with losing both chambers of Congress , leaving Trump without unified Republican control in the legislative branch for the final two years of his presidency.

Emmer, who won a seventh term representing Minnesota’s 6th Congressional District earlier this month, will serve as minority whip in the next Congress. He signaled a willingness to work with Democrats but questioned whether the incoming majorities would follow through on their campaign promises to bring down costs.

“There should be a joint effort to resolve these problems,” he said. “The new Democrat majorities that are coming in, they campaigned on affordability, but that’s what they’re going to have to deliver. And right now, it doesn’t look like that’s what their focus is.”

The Minnesota Republican also weighed in on the war with Iran, describing the nine-month conflict as a “stalemate” despite Trump’s repeated declarations of victory. He defended the president’s efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon but stressed the need to bring the conflict to an end and restore peace in the region.

“When it comes to the war, if it is a war, I don’t know what it is right now — it seems more like a stalemate,” he said.

Looking ahead to the next election cycle in 2028, Emmer said Republicans need to give Americans a reason to vote for them.

“I think the bigger issue for Republicans is we need to reestablish our identity as to who we are and what we offer,” he said. “We got to be for something.”

articles.summary: La inusual imagen ha sorprendido hasta en la emisión en directo de 'La 1'
articles.body: Hay imagenes que hablan por si solas. Una de ellas no ha pasado inadvertida y se ha dado en los momentos previos a que arranque el 'Debate a cuatro' en la Academia de Televisión situada en Tres Cantos (Madrid). Una posición que ocupaban los cuatro dirigentes en el momento en el que los medios gráficos les hacían las fotos oficiales con María Casado, presentadora del debate. Todo ocurría cuando se posicionaban de izquierda a derecha Ada Colau, del Frente Amplio; Alberto Núñez Feijóo, del Partido Popular; Pedro Sánchez, del Partido Socialista; y Santiago Abascal, de Vox. En ese momento, era llamativa la diferencia que había entre Abascal y Sánchez, que por sorteo habían quedado cerca, pero con una distancia apreciable respecto a la que mantenían Feijóo y Colau. Ha sido en el momento en el que estaban haciendo la foto cuando hasta Pepa Bueno, presentadora de RTVE de la programación especial que hacía la cadena pública en los debates en las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. "Llamaba la atención a la mesa, la distancia a la que se había colocado...", llegó a afirmar cuando la producción de este debate ofrecía esta imagen. Unas palabras que matizó: "Bueno, no es tanto, visto... en este plano no es tan significativa la distancia entre Sánchez y Abascal, ¿no? Parecía que se veía mayor", preguntó a los componentes de la mesa que analizaban el debate. Aunque no terminaría ahí. "Pero es mayor que la que hay entre Feijóo y Colau ¿no?", le respondía. Ante un cambio de la imágen Pepa Bueno rectificaba lo que decía: "Y yo creo que un pelín más ancha de la que separa al presidente del Gobierno con Abascal. En este plano... en este plano sí parece..." Y Antón Losada apoyaba la tesis para zanjar este momento: "Marcar las distancias".

articles.title: Trump takes on Somali welfare dependency in Thanksgiving message, lays out who should stay in US
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says only 2% of Minnesota's Somali community should stay, claiming on Truth Social the rest should be thrown out to save the state.
articles.body: In a lengthy Thanksgiving message on Truth Social Thursday, President Donald Trump praised a small fraction of the Somali community, saying they should be allowed to remain in the United States, while calling for the immediate removal of those receiving government assistance while unemployed. The holiday post mixed praise for "AMERICAN PATRIOTS" with criticism of the "Radical Far Left" and Minnesota’s Somali community, which Trump has frequently accused of public assistance fraud in the state. "I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance," Trump wrote in the post. "These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately, thereby saving the Great State of Minnesota, which has no chance if they are allowed to stay." SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME Trump’s remarks echo ongoing criticism from some Republicans regarding public benefit usage and fraud cases within the community. During a House Oversight Committee hearing in January, Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, highlighted data on government support programs, noting that 54% of Somali-headed households in Minnesota receive food stamps. SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD HAS NEFARIOUS TERRORISM LINKS, TOP AGRICULTURE WATCHDOG WARNS CONGRESS Elsewhere in the post, Trump claimed that "murderers, drug dealers, and criminals" — who he said illegally entered the U.S. from foreign prisons and mental institutions — have largely been deported. "They are mostly gone now, brought back to their point of origin and, hopefully, living a beautiful and idyllic life, and promising, ideally, never to kill innocent people again," he wrote. TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE' "We won’t have to worry about that, because they are GONE — but, Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from Faraway Lands," he added. "We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!" Secretary of State Marco Rubio also shared a holiday message on social media, with a video focused on opportunities provided by the U.S. "We know how special this country is. It's the place that gave us freedom. It's a place that gave us opportunity. It's a place that's given our parents, our grandparents, and many of you the chance not just to do well in life, but to leave our children better off than ourselves," Rubio said in the video. articles.title: Santiago Abascal, tajante con Ada Colau después de que le cortara en el turno inicial: "Hay que respetar las normas"
articles.standfirst: Se había pactado no interrumpir en la primera intervención
articles.summary: Se había pactado no interrumpir en la primera intervención
articles.body: Este jueves, 26 de noviembre, se está celebrando el debate electoral a cuatro de las elecciones generales de 2026, lo que supone el último encuentro televisado entre los principales candidatos antes de los comicios del próximo domingo, 29 de noviembre. Organizado por la Academia de Televisión y moderado por María Casado en Madrid Content City (Tres Cantos), reúne a Pedro Sánchez (PSOE), Alberto Núñez Feijóo (PP), Santiago Abascal (Vox) y Ada Colau (Frente Amplio). El primer rifirrafe ha surgido ha tenido como protagonistas a Santiago Abascal y a Ada Colau. En la intervención inicial se había pactado no interrumpir; sin embargo, la máxima figura de Frente Amplio cortó al líder de Vox al no condenar la violencia machista. Y es que, el inicio del discurso de la política catalana había comenzado recordando a la última mujer asesinada por violencia de género. “¿No va a condenar usted la violencia machista?”, le preguntaba Colau cortando a Abascal. “Hay que respetar las normas”, le contestaba el representante de la formación verde, después de que la moderadora, María Casado, recordara que en esta primera toma de contacto no se podía interrumpir. El debate tiene una duración prevista de unas dos horas y se divide en cinco bloques de 20 minutos cada uno, en los que cada candidato dispone de cinco minutos individuales: Vivienda; Economía y fiscalidad; Política social y servicios públicos; Lucha contra la corrupción y regeneración democrática; y Migración y política exterior. La señal institucional se emite de forma simultánea en las principales cadenas nacionales en abierto, plataformas digitales y televisiones autonómicas:La 1, Canal 24 Horas, TVE Internacional, Antena 3, laSexta, Telecinco, Cuatro y La Séptima. Además, también se podrá seguir en las cadenas autonómicas.
